$comment: wa-a11y guided manual Assessment checklist, AGPL-3.0-or-later, Copyright (C) 2026 Kevin Miller (rockypod). Items a person checks that automated tools cannot prove. Plain language; WCAG 2.2 only; level = the primary (first) SC's level, matching web/app/wcag.py. Advisory items are good practice, not conformance requirements. Reviewer notes must never contain personal data.

items.title: Use the whole page with just a keyboard
items.purpose: Find anything a mouse user can do that a keyboard user cannot.
items.instructions: Put the mouse away. Use Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space and the arrow keys to reach and use every control: links, buttons, forms, menus, media. Do not use a mouse at all.
items.observe: Every control can be reached with Tab, and can be used with Enter, Space or arrows. Nothing is only usable with a mouse. For Level AAA, there are no exceptions at all.
items.evidence: Note any control you could reach but not use, and what happened instead.

items.title: Check you can always leave with the keyboard
items.purpose: Make sure keyboard users are never stuck.
items.instructions: Tab into each part of the page (including any dialog, media player or embedded content). Then try to Tab or press Esc to leave it again.
items.observe: Focus always moves out again with Tab, Shift+Tab or Esc. You are never trapped.
items.evidence: Name the part of the page that held focus, and what key failed to leave it.

items.title: Check the focus order makes sense
items.purpose: Focus should follow the reading order people expect.
items.instructions: Tab through the whole page and watch where focus lands each time.
items.observe: The order matches the visual and reading order of the page. If focus jumps somewhere unexpected, note where from and to.
items.evidence: Describe any jump: from which item to which item, and why it felt wrong.

items.title: Check focus is easy to see
items.purpose: Keyboard users must always know where they are.
items.instructions: Tab through the page and look for the focus indicator at every stop.
items.observe: Every focusable thing shows a clear change when focused, at least 3 pixels thick and not cut off by anything. It is obvious where you are.
items.evidence: Name any element whose focus was faint, thin, cut off, or invisible.

items.title: Check nothing covers the focused thing
items.purpose: Sticky headers, popups or ads can hide the focused control.
items.instructions: Tab through the page at 400% zoom and with the page scrolled, watching for sticky bars or overlays.
items.observe: The focused control is never covered at all. If something partly covers it, note whether the whole control was still readable.
items.evidence: Name the sticky or fixed element that covered focus, if any.

items.title: Check dragging has another way
items.purpose: Things you drag (sliders, sortable lists, maps) need a keyboard or button way too.
items.instructions: Find anything you can drag. Try to do the same thing without dragging: with arrow keys, buttons, or a text field.
items.observe: Every drag action has a single-pointer or keyboard alternative that works.
items.evidence: Name the drag control and the alternative you used (or found missing).

items.title: Check controls are big enough to hit
items.purpose: Small targets are hard for shaky hands.
items.instructions: Look at buttons, links, checkboxes and small icon controls. Measure or estimate their clickable size.
items.observe: Controls are at least 24 by 24 pixels, or have enough empty space around them. Note the ones that are smaller.
items.evidence: List controls smaller than 24 px and their measured size.

items.title: Check the page at 320 pixels
items.purpose: People zoom to 400%; the page must not force sideways scrolling.
items.instructions: Zoom the page to 400% (or set the window to 320 pixels wide) and read down the whole page.
items.observe: No sideways scrolling except for things like maps, tables or code. All text stays readable in one column.
items.evidence: Note anything you had to scroll sideways to read, and how far it went.

items.title: Check the reading level
items.purpose: Text should be understandable without secondary-school reading skills.
items.instructions: Take the main body text (not legal or technical quotes). Check the style: short sentences, common words, explained terms. A rough tool check is a hint, not a proof.
items.observe: Main text reads like plain language after removing unusual words. If a formulaic check is used, treat it as a hint only and record it as such.
items.evidence: Record what you judged: paragraphs checked, and your plain-language reasoning.

items.title: Check link text on its own
items.purpose: A screen reader user often jumps link-to-link, out of context.
items.instructions: Read every link text on its own, as a list. For links with unclear text like 'click here', read them again in context.
items.observe: Most links make sense alone. For Level AAA, every link must make sense on its own, out of context.
items.evidence: List link texts that only made sense in context, and the sentence that saved them.

items.title: Check headings and labels describe their topic
items.purpose: Headings and labels set expectations for what follows.
items.instructions: Look at each heading and form label. Does it tell you what the section or field is about, before you read further?
items.observe: Headings and labels are clear and specific, not vague like 'More info'.
items.evidence: List vague headings or labels you found.

items.title: Check you can tell where you are
items.purpose: People should know which page they are on.
items.instructions: Land on a deep page (from a link or search). Can you tell what site and what page you are on, without hunting?
items.observe: The page title, heading or breadcrumb tells you where you are.
items.evidence: Note what cue you used, or what was missing.

items.title: Check names and roles with a screen reader
items.purpose: Buttons, fields and menus must say what they are and what they do.
items.instructions: With a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver or Orca), go through every form control, button, link and custom widget. Listen to what it announces: name, role and value/state. For controls with a visible label, check the accessible name contains the visible text.
items.observe: Every control announces a sensible name, its role, and its state (like 'checked'). Nothing says just 'button' with no name. Visible labels match what is announced.
items.evidence: List controls with missing or wrong names, wrong roles, or states that did not change when used.

items.title: Check status messages are announced
items.purpose: Results and errors that appear should be spoken without moving focus.
items.instructions: Do things that make messages appear (submit a form with errors, save settings). With a screen reader running, listen for the message.
items.observe: The message is announced without the focus jumping somewhere unhelpful.
items.evidence: Note each message: announced, silent, or focus moved unexpectedly.

items.title: Check captions on recorded video
items.purpose: Deaf users need captions and, where needed, audio description.
items.instructions: Play any recorded video. Turn captions on. Check they cover all speech and important sounds. If visual action is not clear from sound alone, check audio description.
items.observe: Captions match the speech, identify speakers, and include key sounds. Audio description exists where needed.
items.evidence: For each video: captions present and correct? description present or not needed?

items.title: Check live captions
items.purpose: Live events need live captions too.
items.instructions: If the page offers a live stream or webinar, join and check captions appear in real time.
items.observe: Captions appear and track the speaker closely enough to follow.
items.evidence: Note the event, caption quality, and delay.

items.title: Check audio-only content has a transcript
items.purpose: Audio clips and video-only clips need a text alternative.
items.instructions: Find audio-only clips or silent video clips. Check a transcript or text description is offered.
items.observe: Every audio-only clip has a transcript; every silent video has a text description.
items.evidence: List clips missing alternatives.

items.title: Check time limits can be turned off
items.purpose: Session timeouts and carousels can cut people off mid-task.
items.instructions: Find anything with a time limit: a session warning, carousel, quiz timer. Look for a way to turn it off, extend it, or adjust it.
items.observe: Time limits can be turned off or extended, or the content warns you before time runs out. For Level AAA, no time limits at all.
items.evidence: Name each time limit and what control you had over it.

items.title: Check people are warned about timeouts
items.purpose: Idle timeouts should be told to users who may lose work.
items.instructions: Find session timeouts. Is the length of inactivity written anywhere, in words, before it happens?
items.observe: The timeout is described in the text, including how long it is.
items.evidence: Note what the page says about timeouts, or nothing.

items.title: Check moving things can be paused
items.purpose: Carousels, tickers and blinking content distract and can be unreadable.
items.instructions: Find anything that moves, blinks, scrolls or auto-plays for more than 5 seconds. Look for a pause, stop or hide control. (wa-a11y itself never animates.)
items.observe: Every moving thing has a working pause, stop or hide control, or it stops within 5 seconds.
items.evidence: Name each moving element and the control you found (or did not).

items.title: Check audio can be stopped
items.purpose: Auto-playing audio fights with screen reader speech.
items.instructions: Find audio that starts on its own. Is there a way to pause or stop it, or turn the volume down, without hunting for it?
items.observe: No audio plays automatically, or there is a stop control right where you need it.
items.evidence: Note the audio and the control you found.

items.title: Check errors are explained in text
items.purpose: People must know what went wrong and how to fix it.
items.instructions: Fill forms wrong on purpose: leave required fields empty, type a wrong format. Read the error messages.
items.observe: Each error says in words what went wrong and which field, not just a colour change. Where possible it says how to fix it.
items.evidence: For each error: the message text, and whether it named the field and the fix.

items.title: Check forms say what they want
items.purpose: Fields need labels, and unusual fields need instructions.
items.instructions: Go through each form field. Is it labelled? If a field needs a format (like a date), are instructions or an example given? Check the page says its language, and marks foreign-language passages.
items.observe: Every field has a visible label. Format hints are in text. Page language is set; other languages are marked.
items.evidence: List unlabelled fields, missing hints, and any language marking you checked.

items.title: Check important submissions can be undone
items.purpose: For consequential actions, people need a chance to check before it is final.
items.instructions: Submit something meaningful (a report, a delete). Can you review, undo, or confirm before it goes through?
items.observe: Actions can be reviewed or confirmed before submission, or undone after.
items.evidence: Note each action and what safety net it had.

items.title: Check you never retype what you already told the page
items.purpose: Being asked to re-enter known information is a memory tax.
items.instructions: Go through a multi-step form. Does it ask again for something you already entered or selected?
items.observe: Nothing is asked twice that the page already knows, except for safety (like password confirmation).
items.evidence: Note what was asked twice.

items.title: Check sign-in is not a puzzle
items.purpose: Memory tests and puzzles block some users from signing in at all.
items.instructions: Try the sign-in flow. Look for cognitive tests: remember a password you typed? recognise pictures? solve a puzzle? Is there another way, or is none needed?
items.observe: Sign-in does not require remembering, transcribing or solving anything cognitive. For Level AAA, there are no cognitive-function exceptions.
items.evidence: Note what the sign-in asked for, and any alternative path.

items.title: Check help is in the same place every time
items.purpose: Help should live in one predictable spot across pages.
items.instructions: Visit several pages. Look for the help/contact link each time.
items.observe: Help appears in the same place on every page, or a link to it does. If there is no help, note that too.
items.evidence: Describe where help was on each page you tried.

items.title: Check the page's language is set
items.purpose: Screen readers need to know the language to pronounce words.
items.instructions: View the page source or use a tool: is the html tag's lang attribute set to the right language?
items.observe: The page declares its language correctly.
items.evidence: Record the lang value you saw.

items.title: Check text is real text
items.purpose: Text in images cannot zoom, reflow, or be read aloud properly.
items.instructions: Look for pictures that contain words (banners, buttons, screenshots of text).
items.observe: Real text is used instead of images of words, except logos or where unavoidable. For Level AAA, no images of words at all.
items.evidence: List images that contain words and what each says.

items.title: Check blocks of text are easy to read
items.purpose: Long text blocks need good spacing and width for comfortable reading.
items.instructions: Find blocks of text over 250 characters. Check: width under 80 characters, lines not justified, spacing between lines, and colours you can pick (if offered).
items.observe: Text blocks are under 80 characters wide, left-aligned, with breathing room. Nothing is justified or cramped.
items.evidence: Note what you measured and anything that failed.
